title: Amino Acid Decarboxylase Test (Lysine/Ornithine/Arginine)
principle: Organisms possessing the relevant decarboxylase enzyme (lysine decarboxylase, ornithine decarboxylase, or arginine dihydrolase) remove the carboxyl group from the corresponding amino acid, producing an alkaline amine end product that shifts a pH indicator (commonly bromocresol purple) from yellow back to purple under the anaerobic, mineral-oil-sealed conditions of the test broth.
purpose: Widely used, particularly for Enterobacteriaceae and related Gram-negative rods, as part of a biochemical identification panel to differentiate genera and species based on which amino acid(s) they can decarboxylate.
reagents: Decarboxylase base broth with the target amino acid (lysine, ornithine, or arginine) and a pH indicator

procedure.instruction: Inoculate the amino-acid-containing broth (and a control broth without added amino acid) with the test organism.
Overlay each tube with a layer of sterile mineral oil to create anaerobic conditions, which favor the decarboxylation reaction over competing oxidative pathways.
Incubate at the appropriate temperature for the manufacturer- or method-specified period.
Observe the color of the broth against the un-amino-acid control.

positiveResult: The broth turns/remains purple (alkaline), indicating decarboxylation and an alkaline amine end product.
negativeResult: The broth turns or remains yellow (acidic), indicating fermentation of the base medium without a subsequent alkaline shift.
interpretation: A positive result must be read against the amino-acid-free control tube, which should turn yellow from glucose fermentation alone; a positive amino-acid tube that stays purple confirms decarboxylase activity rather than simply weak initial acidification.
precautions: Always run the amino-acid-free control broth in parallel — without it, a positive result cannot be confidently distinguished from simple glucose fermentation.
Ensure the mineral oil overlay is complete and continuous to maintain anaerobic conditions.
limitations: Reaction timing can vary by organism and specific amino acid, and some results are read at 24 and 48 hours to catch delayed reactions.
This is a single biochemical character and is interpreted alongside other tests, not used alone for identification.
